I do not know with which of the two he concluded: ﴿then in what speech after it will they believe?﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, 'Bow down,' they do not bow down.﴾" [al-Mursalat: 50]

Its verses number fifty, without disagreement. Its connection with what precedes it is that when Allah, glorified is He, said earlier ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Insan: 31], etc., He opened this surah with an oath upon what indicates its realization, and the mention of its time and its signs. It has also been said that He, glorified is He, swore to the realization of everything the surah contained before, of the threat to the disbelievers and the wicked and the promise to the believers and the righteous. So He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By those sent forth successively﴾ ﴿then those that blow with violence﴾ ﴿and those that spread widely﴾ ﴿then those that separate decisively﴾ ﴿then those that deliver a reminder﴾

It has been said that He, glorified is He, swore by those of the angels whom He chose, peace be upon them, according to what 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid. It is said that "al-Mursalat" and "al-'Asifat" are one group, and "al-Nashirat," "al-Fariqat," and "al-Mulqiyat" are other groups. The first are groups sent by His command, and ordered to carry it out, so they blew with violence in their passage and hastened as the wind blows violently, swiftly in carrying out the command and bringing punishment upon the disbelievers, rescuing the prophets, peace be upon them, and supporting them. The second are groups that spread their wings in the air as they descended with revelation, and so they separated between truth and falsehood, and thus delivered a reminder to the prophets, peace be upon them. Perhaps the one who delivers the reminder to them is not limited to Gabriel, peace be upon him, but is rather their chief, and what indicates this is the hadith of al-Rasd and what is in some reports: "An angel came down to me with a message from my Lord, placing one foot in the sky and the other between my hands."

So "al-Mursalat" is a qualifier of an omitted noun, and the meaning is "and every group sent." Likewise "(al-Nashirat)." "'Urfan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and the meaning is "in succession." The original would have been "and those sent forth in succession, like the mane," and that is the mane of an animal such as a horse or a hyena, I mean the hair known on its nape. He omitted "in succession," since the comparison indicates it, and then he omitted the particle of comparison for emphasis. From this comes the saying "they came 'urfan wahidan" when they come one following another, and they are upon him like the mane of the hyena when they gather against him.

It is understood from the words of some that "al-'urf" originally meant what was mentioned, then its use in the sense of succession became common, so it became a conventional literal usage in it. Or it is a direct object of cause, meaning "by the 'urf," which is the opposite of "nukr" (what is unknown), that is, ﴿and those sent forth﴾ for goodness and what is known. It is not an objection to this that the sending is for the punishment of the disbelievers, because if that is not known to them, it is known to the prophets, peace be upon them, and to the believers, for whose sake Allah, exalted is He, took vengeance upon them. The conjunction of "al-Nashirat" with what precedes it by "wa" is evident, since the two differ in essence. The conjunction of "al-'Asifat" with "al-Mursalat," and "al-Fariqat" with "al-Nashirat," and likewise what follows them with "fa," is to treat the difference of attributes as the difference of essences, as in his saying:

"Ya lahfa Ziyadata lil-Harithi al-Sabihi fa-al-Ghanimi fa-al-Ayibi"

It is for indicating the order of the meanings of the attributes in existence, that is, the one who raided at dawn, then took booty, then returned. The order of the passage of the command after the sending, and the command to rescue, is evident. As for the order of delivering the reminder to the prophets, peace be upon them, after the distinction between truth and falsehood, while it is evident that the distinction comes later than the delivering, it has been said that this is because the distinction is interpreted as His will, and then it precedes the delivering. It has also been said that the distinction precedes the delivering without any need to interpret it as His will, because by the very descent of them with revelation, which is the truth opposed to falsehood, which is desire and corrupt opinion, the distinction occurs, and only the knowledge of it comes later.

From this it appears that the distinction is ordered after the spreading of the wings, since what results from it is that they spread their wings to descend, then they descended, then they delivered. This is not evident in relation to what precedes it, because the will to distinguish accompanies the spreading, and likewise its will if interpreted, according to the apparent meaning. Rather it may be said that this will is prior. It has also been said that the "fa" in that is for relative ordering, since the will to distinguish is higher in rank than the spreading. It has also been said that it is in this and in what follows it merely to signal that each of the mentioned attributes, I mean the spreading and the distinguishing, independently indicates the deserving of the groups described by them, for the sake of exalting and honoring them through the oath by them, for if they had been mentioned in the order of occurrence, it might have been understood that the combined three in sequence is what necessitates the deserving mentioned.

The use of "al-'Asifat" in the sense of those hastening with the speed of the wind is a metaphor by way of metaphor. It is not far-fetched that "al-'Asifat" may mean those that destroy and annihilate with the punishment with which they were sent against those to whom they were sent, also by way of metaphor, or by way of the sent metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 6:

"Udhran (ʿudhran) and nudhran (nudhran)" in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿ʿUdhran aw nudhran﴾ (Or as excuses or warnings). It is permitted that both be verbal nouns (maṣdar): from ʿadhara, when he removed wrongdoing (al-isāʾa), and from andhara, when he warned (khawwafa). Both come on the pattern fuʿl, like shukr and kufr. The first is apparent, because fuʿl is among the verbal nouns of the triliteral verb. As for the second, it is against the analogical rule, since the verbal noun of afʿala is ifʿāl. It has also been said that it is an ism al-maṣdar (noun of the verbal action), like ṭāqa, or that it is the maṣdar of nadhara with the meaning of andhara, and this is tolerated in what preceded. It is also possible that both are plurals of ʿadhīr, meaning apology (maʿdhira), and nadhīr, meaning warning (indhār). Their accusative status is that of the purpose clause (ʿilliyya), and the governing element for both is "al-mulqiyāt" (the ones that cast), or "dhikran" (remembrance), which means admonition and exhortation through encouragement and warning. That is, ﴿fal-mulqiyāti dhikran﴾ (then those that cast down a reminder), for the sake of excuse for the righteous, or for the sake of warning for the falsifiers. Or they are in the state of being (ḥāl) from "al-mulqiyāt" or from the pronoun concealed within it, in the sense of: excusing or warning. Or they are in apposition (badal) to ﴿dhikran﴾, on the basis that by it is meant revelation, so they would be a partial apposition (badal baʿḍ); or the reminder and admonition, so they would be a total apposition (badal kull). And if they are two adjectives meaning excusing and warning, then their accusative is in the state (ḥāl) only.

The particle "aw" (or) in all of this is for enumeration (tanwīʿ), not for alternation (tardīd). Therefore al-Dinawari, in Mushkil al-Qur'an (Problems of the Qur'an), said that it means "wa" (and). It has been said that the second group are the groups that spread the laws over the earth, up to the end of what preceded. The basis of the coordination is that what is meant is that they intended to spread, so they descended and then cast. Interpretation was needed because of the casting being to the prophets, peace be upon them; otherwise it does not need it in the spreading and the separating, since the order of separating after spreading is evident. Thus it has been said, so do not be heedless. It has also been said: groups that spread souls dead through disbelief and ignorance, with what they revealed, so they separated, etc. And spreading on this view means giving life, while in what preceded it means dissemination.

It has been said: there is no difference among all of them except by their attributes, and they are all from among the angels according to the earlier opinions. However, this speaker did not take into account the interpretation of spreading as spreading of wings, and said: God, glorified is He, swore by groups of angels whom He sent, mighty and majestic, with His commands in succession, so they blow forcefully like the winds in obedience, and spread the laws over the earth; or they spread souls dead through ignorance, with what they revealed of knowledge, so they separated between truth and falsehood, and then cast to the prophets a reminder. Its apparent meaning is also that the sending to the prophets was with the laws, of commands and prohibitions, on the basis that "awāmir" (commands) is a plural of a plural specific to command as opposed to prohibition, so in his words there is sufficiency.

The command was singled out for mention. It has been said that this is because it is more important, although it does not convey what is meant of prohibition by its form, such as "da" (leave) for example. It has also been said, regarding the coordination of "al-nāshirāt" with "wa" rather than "fa", and the coordination of "al-fāriqāt" with it, that spreading on this view means dissemination of the laws, and this occurs after revelation, preaching and acceptance, and requires time; therefore "wa" was used and it was not joined with the sequential "fa". When spreading occurs, separation follows it without delay. It should not be thought that the spreading ought to be "then" (thumma) at that point, because intention here is not connected with delay. The matter remains of why the spreading of laws or the spreading of souls and the separation are mentioned before the casting, although they are after it in reality. It has been said that this indicates that each of them is a goal of the casting, which is worthy of attention, or that it signals that each of the attributes independently indicates the deserving of glorification, as you have heard. Moreover, the scope of interpretation is wide, so reflect.

It has been said: God, glorified is He, swore by individuals of two types of winds. So a qualified noun is supposed for "al-mursalāt" and another qualified noun for "al-nāshirāt". By "al-mursalāt" is meant the winds sent for punishment, because sending is commonly used for it; and by "al-nāshirāt" are the winds of mercy. The summary is that He, majestic and exalted, swore by winds of punishment that He sent, so they blew forcefully, and winds of mercy that spread the clouds in the atmosphere, so they separated them over the regions, and then cast a reminder, either as an excuse for those who seek excuse before God, the Exalted, by their repentance and seeking forgiveness, when they witness the signs of His mercy in the rain; or as a warning to those who disbelieve in that and attribute it to the stars and the like. The attribution of the casting of the reminder to them is because they are a cause of its occurrence, if the blessing is thanked through them, or if they are disbelieved. So the figurative usage is in the attribution. And by "ʿurfan" is meant consecutively, or "al-nāshirāt" are winds of mercy that spread the plants and brought them forth, that is, they became a cause for that by spreading the clouds and pouring them down; so they separated each kind from the rest by shape, color and all other properties, and thus caused a reminder, either as an excuse for the grateful or as a warning for the disbelievers.

It has been said: God swore first by the winds, and second by clouds that spread the dead earth, so they separated between one who gives thanks and one who disbelieves, like His words ﴿Surely We would have given them abundant water﴾ ﴿that We might test them therein﴾ [al-Jinn: 16, 17]. So they caused a reminder, either ... or ...

It has been said: God, may He be exalted and majestic, swore by the verses of the Qur'an sent to the Messenger of God ﷺ as grace and kindness, or one thing after another, because it was revealed in parts. So they blew forcefully and removed all other books by abrogation, spread the traces of guidance in the eastern and western parts of the earth, separated between truth and falsehood, and then cast the mention of truth upon the shoulders of the worlds.

It has been said: God, majestic in majesty, swore by His messengers from among mankind, who were sent as kindness and grace, as is the correct position, not as an obligation, as one who claims claims. They were strengthened, their affair became great, they spread their religion and what they brought, and so they separated between truth and falsehood, and lawful and unlawful, and cast a reminder among those under obligation. It is permitted, on this view, that "ʿurfan" be understood as consecutive.

It has been said: God, Blessed and Exalted, swore by complete souls, that is, created in the attribute of perfection and readiness to accept what they were charged with and created for, sent as kindness to bodies for their perfection; so they blew forcefully and removed whatever is other than truth by considering the true proofs, and so they separated between the established truth which subsists by its essence and to which nothing else contributes, which is the Necessarily Existent, glorified is He, and between falsehood which is non-existent in itself. They saw everything perishing except His Face, and so they cast into the hearts and tongues and established therein His remembrance, so that there is nothing in their hearts and tongues but His remembrance, mighty and majestic; or they removed the remembrance of other than Him, glorified is He, from the hearts and tongues, so no remembrance of anything besides Him remains in them. It has been said: the first three are the winds, and the last two are the angels, peace be upon them; and it has been said the reverse. The correspondence lies in subtlety and swiftness of movement. It has been said that the first two are the angels, except that "al-mursalāt" are angels of mercy, and "al-ʿāṣifāt" are angels of punishment, and the last three are verses of the Qur'an brought down by the angels.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from one line, from Abu Ṣāliḥ, that he said: "al-mursalāt ʿurfan" are the messengers, sent with kindness; "fal-ʿāṣifāti ʿaṣfan" is the wind; "wal-nāshirāti nashran" is the rain; "fal-fāriqāti farqan" are the messengers. And from another line: "al-mursalāt ʿurfan" are the angels; "fal-ʿāṣifāti ʿaṣfan" are the violent winds; "wal-nāshirāti nashran" are the angels who spread the books, that is, the books of deeds, as has come explicitly in some narrations; "fal-fāriqāti farqan" are the angels who separate between truth and falsehood; "fal-mulqiyāti dhikran" are also the angels who bring the Qur'an and the Book; "ʿudhran aw nudhran" from Him, the Exalted, to mankind, and they are the messengers, who excuse and warn.

And from Abu Ṣāliḥ there are other narrations on this, and likewise from eminent Companions and Successors. From Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra and Muqatil: "al-mursalāt" are the angels, sent with ʿurf, the opposite of nukr, which is revelation.

In another narration from Ibn Mas'ud, they are the winds, and he explained "al-ʿāṣifāt" as those blowing with great intensity. The explanation of "al-mursalāt" as such has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatada. In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, they are the groups of the prophets, sent as bounty from God upon His servants. And from Abu Mas'ud: "al-nāshirāt" are the winds that spread God's mercy and His rain. It is narrated from Mujahid and Qatada. Al-Rabi' said: the angels spread people from their graves.

Al-Dahhak said: the scrolls are spread before God, the Exalted, with the deeds of the servants, and on this view "al-nāshirāt" is in the sense of attribution.

From Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak: "al-fāriqāt" are the angels who separate between truth and falsehood, and lawful and unlawful. Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: the verses of the Qur'an separated between what is lawful and what is unlawful. Also from Mujahid: the winds separate the clouds and so scatter them.

From Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada and the majority: "al-mulqiyāt" are the angels who cast what they carried of revelation to the prophets. From al-Rabi': the verses of the Qur'an. Some people explained "al-ʿāṣifāt" as the destructive signs, such as earthquakes, thunderbolts and others. Some explained "al-fāriqāt" as the rain-bearing clouds, likening them to the pregnant she-camel, al-fārūq, who is the one that wails when she gives birth. Some explained them as the intellects, which separate between truth and falsehood, and sound and corrupt, and so on, among the other narrations and opinions which cannot easily be restricted. What I think most apparent is that the sworn-by thing is two things: "al-mursalāt al-ʿāṣifāt" and "al-nāshirāt al-fāriqāt al-mulqiyāt", because of the strong apparent coordination by "wa" in that, and because all of them are of the kind of wind, since this is more suitable to the context, which includes the matter of resurrection and dispersal, since the observed effects which follow the winds, both near and remote, call out with the loudest voice, until it nearly resembles the sound of the trumpet blast, indicating the possibility of that and its truth, and its being within the scope of God's will and His great power. Nevertheless, the opinions are numerous before you, and you are not denied; so choose for yourself what is sweet to you.

ʿIsa read "ʿurufan" with two dammas, like nukur in nukr. Ibn ʿAbbas read "fal-mullaqiyāt" with shaddah, from talqiyah, and it has been said that talqiyah is like iliqāʾ, the conveying of speech to the addressee; one says "laqqaytuhu al-dhikr" and he received it. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that he, may God be pleased with him, read "fal-mulaqqayāt" with fatḥah on the lām and shaddah on the qāf, as an ism maf'ūl, meaning "delivered (mulaqqayah) from God, mighty and majestic." Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Kharija, Talha, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, ʿIsa, al-Hasan (with variation), and al-Aʿmash from Abu Bakr read "ʿudhuran aw nudhuran" with dammah on both dhāl.

The two Haramis, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Bakr, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Shayba and Abu Ja'far also read, with sukun on the dhāl in "ʿudhran" and dammah in "nudhuran". Ibrahim al-Taymi read "wa-nudhuran" with a waw.

"And His saying, ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely going to occur.﴾ is the response to the oath. And "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), even though it is written joined (to "inna"); the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) is omitted, meaning: indeed, that which you are promised of the coming of the Resurrection is certainly going to occur without doubt. It is also permissible that by the relative pronoun is meant everything that the preceding surah contained, but this is very far from the apparent meaning."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 8:

﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾. Their trace is removed, either by removing their light or by annihilating their very essence and eliminating them entirely. Both of these matters will happen, and there is nothing impossible about them in any way. What the earlier philosophers (al-Falasifah) claimed concerning those celestial bodies, namely the impossibility of their dissolution and annihilation, is weaker than a spider's web. As for what the later ones among them (al-Mu'asirun) claimed about them, although it is not established for us, the possibility of their being obliterated is evident in the highest degree.

﴿And when the sky is split open﴾: it is cleaved, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿When the sky is split asunder﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1]; ﴿And the day the sky will be split apart with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It was also said that it is opened, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And the sky will be opened and will become gates﴾ [al-Naba': 19]. Sibawayh recited:

*The one who opens the gate of the amir, the obscure one*

There is nothing preventing this either, whether the sky is a solid body or a subtle body. The proofs that rending and rejoining are impossible in it are that it contains rifts that do not close.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 10:

﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾ — they are made like the wool that is scattered by the winnowing-fork (al-minsaf) and the like. ﴿And the mountains are pulverized into powder﴾ ﴿and the mountains become scattered sand, poured out﴾. Al-Alusi says, quoting al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan): "The winds scatter them, and that is after they are set in motion." It is also said that it means their being made into dust (habaʾ). It is also said that "nusifat" means they are taken from their places swiftly, from "intasaftu al-shay'" meaning "I snatched the thing away" when one seizes it.

ʿAmr ibn Maymun read "tummassat" and "furrijat" with doubled mim and ra' (shaddah). Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, mentioned that all three verbs were read with the shaddah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 11:

﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾. That is, they are made to reach the appointed time they were awaiting, which is the Day of Resurrection. It is also permissible that the meaning is: a time is set for them at which they attend to bear witness against the nations.
Page 173
This occurs when it arrives and takes place. The preferred view is the first, as Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said. Its clarification, as in al-Kashf (of al-Zamakhshari), is that tawqit (appointing a time) of a thing means defining it and specifying its time. So its application to the persons (dhawat) requires an implied elision, because what is timed (al-mu'aqqat) is the events (al-ahdath), not the bodies (al-juthath). It also comes in the sense of making a thing reach its defined time, and in this case it applies directly to them without elision, if there is a connection (mulabasa) between them and that time. It is the preferred view because the Resurrection is not a time in which the time of the messengers, when they attend to bear witness, is specified; rather it is that very time itself. ﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾ requires this, because when you say "If you honour me, I will honour you," it implies that the time of the addressee honouring the speaker is what the particle "idha" indicates. Whether the adverb is taken as its complement or the complement of the conditional response, there must be an interpretation, and this has been pointed out within the course of the commentary.

Al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Isa and Khalid read «uqqitat» with a hamza and a light qaf. Abu al-Ashhab, Amr ibn Ubayd, Abu Amr and also Isa read «wuqqitat» with a waw, in accordance with the original form, because the hamza is substituted for a waw that bears a permanent damma, and this is a regular process as explained in its proper place.

Isa said: "wuqqitat" is the dialect of Lower Mudar. Abdullah ibn al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read «wuqatat» with a single waw and a light qaf. Al-Hasan also read «wuwqitat» with two waws in the pattern fa'walat. In all of what has preceded, "idha" is a conditional particle.

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For what Day were they deferred?﴾ It has been said that it is a quoted statement (maqul) of a suppressed utterance (qawl muqaddar), which is the answer to "when" (idha), meaning: it will be said, "For what Day were they deferred?" and so on. He took "deferral" (ta'jil) to mean "postponement" (ta'khir), from the expression "a debt is deferred" (dayn mu'ajjal), as opposed to "immediate" (al-hal). The pronoun refers to what the context implies, and the interrogative is for the sake of magnifying and expressing wonder at the terror of that Day, meaning: when such and such is the case, it will be said, "For what Day were the matters connected with the Messengers postponed?", namely the punishment and humiliation of the disbelievers, the honouring and care of the believers, and the manifestation of what the Messengers, peace be upon them, used to mention of the Hereafter, its conditions, the dreadfulness of its affairs and its terrors.

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the matters alluded to earlier: the extinguishing of the stars, the splitting of the sky, the blowing away of the mountains, and the appointing of a time for the Messengers. It is also permissible that it refers to the Messengers, though the meaning is as previously stated. It has been said that the suppressed utterance may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "were appointed" (uqqitat), meaning: while being said about them, "For what Day were they deferred?" It is also possible that the sentence itself, without a suppressed utterance, occupies the position of the second object of "were appointed", taking it to mean "were informed", as if it were said: "And when the Messengers were informed of the time of their deferral", meaning of its coming and occurrence.

The answer to "when" (idha) on both interpretations has been said to be His saying, Exalted is He, to come, ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾, and the omission of the particle "fa" (fa'") has occurred in similar constructions.

It has also been said that the answer is omitted, being indicated by the context, meaning: "the Decision has occurred" or "what you were promised has occurred." Abu Hayyan chose this view. It is also permissible, on the supposition that the answer is ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾, or on the supposition that the suppressed element is placed later, that the clause ﴿For what Day were they deferred?﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) to magnify the matter of that Day.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 13–14:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For a Day of Decision﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿For what Day were they postponed?﴾, explaining it. It has also been said that it is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: "They were postponed for the Day of Decision between creation." ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ That is: what thing made you able to know what it is? This is on the basis that the first "mā" is a subject (mubtada') and "adrāka" is its predicate, while the second "mā" is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam) and "yawm" is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), not the reverse, as Sibawayh preferred. This is because the focus of the benefit is the explanation that the Day of Decision is a extraordinary matter whose measure cannot be estimated and whose reality cannot be fully grasped, as the declarative form of "mā" indicates, not the explanation that the Day of Decision is one of the extraordinary matters, as its reverse would indicate. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to increase the terror and awe that the speech intends.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 13–14:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For a Day of Decision﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿For what Day were they postponed?﴾, explaining it. It has also been said that it is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: "They were postponed for the Day of Decision between creation." ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ That is: what thing made you able to know what it is? Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 15–18:

﴿Woe on that Day to those who deny.﴾ That is, on that terrifying day. "Woe" (wayl) is originally a verbal noun meaning destruction (halak), and its proper case would be the accusative, with a verb of the same root or meaning implied; however, it is put in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada') to indicate the permanence and continuity of the destruction upon the one against whom it is invoked. "That day" (yawma'idhin) is either its adverbial complement (zarf) or its qualifier (sifah), so what justifies beginning with it (the indefinite noun) is evident. The well-known view is that what justifies this is that it is used in supplication, as in ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24].

﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ Such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. Qatadah read "nuhlik" (نَهْلِكِ) with a fatha on the nun, taking it from "halakahu" in the sense of "ahlakahu" (he destroyed him). From this comes "halik" in the sense of "muhlik" (destroying), as is evident in the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

"A desolate wilderness, whoever crosses it, its terrors encompass whoever enters it."

This is so that the particle of the preposition is not joined with the omitted pronoun (i.e., "'anhu aw fihi" would otherwise be needed), and so that it corresponds with what is in the second half of the verse.

﴿Then We shall follow them with the latter ones﴾ with the damma (nutbi'uhum) read as a resumption (isti'naf). It is a threat to the people of Makkah and an informing of what will occur after the Hijrah, such as Badr. It is as if it were said: "Then We will do to their likes among the latter ones what We did to the former, and We will treat them in the same way, because they denied in the same manner as those did." This is reinforced by the reading of 'Abdullah, "thumma sanutbi'uhum" with the sin of future tense. It is also permitted that it be a conjunction upon His statement "Did We not destroy" to its end.

Al-A'raj and al-'Abbas, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read "nutbi'hum" with the sukun on the 'ayn, so it is taken as a jussive and a conjunction upon "nuhlik." In that case the "latter ones" are those who came later in destruction from among those mentioned, such as the people of Lut, Shu'ayb and Musa, peace be upon them, not the disbelievers of Makkah, since they had not yet been destroyed. The conjunction upon "nuhlik" requires this.

It is also permitted that it has been given sukun for lightness, as in ﴿And what will make you aware﴾ [al-An'am: 109]; it is then marfu' as in the reading of the majority, but the damma is presumed. ﴿Thus﴾ like that terrible deed, ﴿We do to the criminals﴾, that is, to everyone who commits crime; the meaning is that Our way is established upon that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 19–23:

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾: that is, the day when We destroy them, ﴿to those who deny﴾ the signs of Allah the Exalted and His prophets, peace be upon them. There is no repetition in this, since the first woe is for the punishment of the Hereafter, and this one is for the punishment of this world.

It has also been said: there is no repetition, because the object of "the deniers" differs in the two places. Here its object is what you have heard, and in what came before it is the Day of Judgment and the like. The same is said of what follows. It has also been permitted to regard them as one and the same, and emphasis is a good thing with no harm in it. ﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾ From a vile, filthy drop. There is no proof in this of the impurity of semen. ﴿Then We placed it in a secure lodging﴾, which is the womb, ﴿for a known term﴾: that is, a known measure of time with Allah the Exalted, which He determined for birth, nine months or less or more than that. ﴿So We determined it﴾: that is, We determined that determination. ﴿How excellent are We as determiners!﴾ That is, how excellent are We as those who determine it.

It has also been permitted that the meaning is: "So We had power over that, and how excellent are We in power over it." The first is preferable, because of the reading of ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, and of Nafi' and al-Kisa'i, "fa-qaddarna" with the doubled letter (shaddah), and because of the Exalted's saying ﴿From a drop He created him and determined him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 19], and because of His saying ﴿for a known term﴾, which magnifies it by making the end-point itself the object of attention. So it is said: "We determined that determination", meaning a determination indicating perfect power and perfect mercy. And the discourse on power is complete with His saying ﴿Did We not create you?﴾. As for al-Tibi's preference for the second, affirming power is preferable, because speaking to deniers has no basis, since no one denies this power; and even if it were granted, they have already acknowledged it by His saying ﴿Did We not create you?﴾. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 24–26:

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers,﴾ meaning: by Our power over that, or over the resurrection (al-i'adah). ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle (kifat)?﴾ Kifat is a noun of kind, or a noun of instrument (ism alah) for that which gathers (yaktifu), meaning it gathers and collects. From kafata al-shay'a, when one gathers and collects it, like al-dimam and al-jima' for that which gathers and collects. They cited the verse of al-Samsama ibn al-Tirimmah:

"You are today alive upon the earth, and tomorrow it will gather you in its kifat."

And on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah, its tafsir is "the vessel" (al-wi'a). And His saying, ﴿alive and dead﴾ is an object (maf'ul) of an omitted verb, not of "kifatan", because the noun of kind, and likewise the noun of instrument, as the grammarians have stated, does not govern. The meaning: Have We not made it a receptacle that gathers and collects many living upon its back and un-counted dead in its belly? It was said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) like al-qital, described by it for emphasis, so it needs no supposed verb. 

It was also said: it is the plural of kafit, like siyam and sa'im, so it too needs no supposed verb; or the plural of kift, with a kasra on the kaf and sukun on the fa', which is a vessel, like qidh and qidah, and it is applied to the earth together with its plurality, while its singularity is considered in terms of its regions.

It is permitted that the two plurals be accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the omitted object of "kifatan", the meaning being: kifatan iyyahum or iyyakum, or kifatan al-insa, ﴿alive and dead﴾. Or from an object whose verb is omitted, meaning: ﴿kifatan﴾ gathering them, or gathering you, or gathering mankind, ﴿alive and dead﴾. And it is possible that their accusative is as objects of "najʻal" with an implied noun: "possessing living and dead." Or that by "amwatan" is meant the dead land (al-ard al-mawat), as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid,
[page 175]
and by "ahya'" what is opposite to it.

The accusative of "kifatan" as a circumstantial state of "al-ard" is possible, but you know that the accusative of both as objects is more apparent, and after it their accusative as circumstantial states of an omitted noun. Their tanwin, as you heard earlier, is for multiplicity. It is permitted that it be for partiality, intending the living humans and their dead, and they are not all the living and the dead; this does not contradict the magnification, considering that it is a part that is not limited and is great in itself, so do not be heedless.

Al-Kiya cited the verse as evidence for the obligation of covering the dead and burying them. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Ibn al-Qasim argued with it for cutting off the hand of the grave-robber (al-nabbash), because He, exalted is He, made the grave for the dead like a house for the living, so it is a protected place (hirz). The weakness of the two inferences is not hidden.

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers,﴾ meaning: by Our power over that, or over the resurrection (al-i'adah). ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle (kifat)?﴾ Kifat is a noun of kind, or a noun of instrument (ism alah) for that which gathers (yaktifu), meaning it gathers and collects. From kafata al-shay'a, when one gathers and collects it, like al-dimam and al-jima' for that which gathers and collects. They cited the verse of al-Samsama ibn al-Tirimmah:

"You are today alive upon the earth, and tomorrow it will gather you in its kifat."

And on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah, its tafsir is "the vessel" (al-wi'a). And His saying, ﴿alive and dead﴾ is an object (maf'ul) of an omitted verb, not of "kifatan", because the noun of kind, and likewise the noun of instrument, as the grammarians have stated, does not govern. The meaning: Have We not made it a receptacle that gathers and collects many living upon its back and un-counted dead in its belly? It was said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) like al-qital, described by it for emphasis, so it needs no supposed verb. 

It was also said: it is the plural of kafit, like siyam and sa'im, so it too needs no supposed verb; or the plural of kift, with a kasra on the kaf and sukun on the fa', which is a vessel, like qidh and qidah, and it is applied to the earth together with its plurality, while its singularity is considered in terms of its regions.

It is permitted that the two plurals be accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the omitted object of "kifatan", the meaning being: kifatan iyyahum or iyyakum, or kifatan al-insa, ﴿alive and dead﴾. Or from an object whose verb is omitted, meaning: ﴿kifatan﴾ gathering them, or gathering you, or gathering mankind, ﴿alive and dead﴾. And it is possible that their accusative is as objects of "najʻal" with an implied noun: "possessing living and dead." Or that by "amwatan" is meant the dead land (al-ard al-mawat), as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid,
[page 175]
and by "ahya'" what is opposite to it.

The accusative of "kifatan" as a circumstantial state of "al-ard" is possible, but you know that the accusative of both as objects is more apparent, and after it their accusative as circumstantial states of an omitted noun. Their tanwin, as you heard earlier, is for multiplicity. It is permitted that it be for partiality, intending the living humans and their dead, and they are not all the living and the dead; this does not contradict the magnification, considering that it is a part that is not limited and is great in itself, so do not be heedless.

Al-Kiya cited the verse as evidence for the obligation of covering the dead and burying them. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Ibn al-Qasim argued with it for cutting off the hand of the grave-robber (al-nabbash), because He, exalted is He, made the grave for the dead like a house for the living, so it is a protected place (hirz). The weakness of the two inferences is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 27:

﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾ i.e., firm mountains, ﴿towering high﴾ i.e., lofty, and from this comes the expression "he lifted his nose high" (shamakha bi-anfihi). The description of the masculine plural with the feminine plural is regular for non-rational beings, as in ﴿months well-known﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. Their indefiniteness (tankir) is either for magnification (tafkhim), or to indicate that there are mountains on the earth that are not known and have not been identified; the earth of God, exalted is He, is vast, and in it is what none knows but God, mighty and majestic.

It has also been said that it is to indicate that among the mountains there are some that are not known, namely the celestial mountains. This agrees with the views of the people of modern philosophy (ahl al-falsafah al-jadidah), who claimed the existence of many mountains on the moon and supposed their existence elsewhere. It has been objected that this is an interpretation by means of what is not known.

﴿And We gave you to drink sweet water﴾ i.e., fresh, sweet water, by creating it in the roots of the mountains and causing it to flow for you from them in rivers, and making it gush forth in springs that draw from what We have deposited in them. It may also be interpreted in a broader sense than this, and [it includes] rain water sent down from the sky.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 28–30:

﴿Woe on that Day to those who deny﴾, [denying] such great blessings. ﴿Proceed﴾, that is, it will be said to them on that Day, for reproach and rebuke: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny﴾ in the world, of the punishment. ﴿Proceed﴾, that is, specifically. So it is not a repetition of the first [command]. It was also said that it is a repetition of it, even though it is restricted by the words of the Exalted: ﴿to a shade﴾, which is the shade of the smoke of Hellfire, as the majority of the exegetes said. So it is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43]. In it there is a mocking metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah). Ruways, from Ya'qub, read «Proceed» in the past tense form, and it is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What followed the command?" So it was said: "Proceed to a shade ﴿with three branches﴾", branching out, because of its immensity, into three branches, as is the nature of the great smoke: you see it spreading out like the locks of hair.

In some reports: "A tongue of fire comes forth and encompasses the disbelievers like a pavilion, and three branches branch out from its smoke, shading them until the reckoning of them is finished, while the believers are in the shade of the Throne."

As for the specificity of the number three, it was said that either it is because the veil of the soul from the lights of holiness consists of the sense, the imagination and the estimative faculty (al-wahm); or because what leads to this punishment is the satanic estimative faculty located in the brain, the beastly irascible faculty (al-quwwah al-ghadabiyyah al-sab'iyyah) which is to the right of the heart, and the bestial appetitive faculty (al-quwwah al-shahwiyyah al-bahimiyyah) which is to its left. For this reason it was said: one branch stands above the disbeliever, one to his right, and one to his left.

It was also said: because their denial of the punishment includes denial of God the Exalted and denial of His Messenger (ﷺ), so there are three denials. Some scholars regarded the denial of the punishment as the root, and the three branches as the two mentioned denials and the denial of clear reason. So reflect. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this is said to the worshippers of the cross, so the believers are in the shade of God, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their deity, which is the cross, which has three branches.

﴿Neither shading﴾, meaning not providing shade. It is a second attribute of ﴿shadow﴾ (ظِلٍّ), and He negated its being a shading thing, since a shadow is only ever shading (ظِلٌّ مُظَلِّلٌ), to indicate that calling it a shadow is a mockery of them. It is also because one might suppose that there is some comfort for them in it, so this possibility is negated by that statement. There is also an implicit suggestion that their shadow is not the shadow of the believers.

﴿Nor will it avail against the blaze﴾, meaning it will not be of any benefit at any time, nor will it ward off anything of the heat of the blaze. The verb yughni (يُغْنِي) is made transitive with min (مِن) because it implies the meaning of yab'udu (يَبْعُدُ), "to keep away."

It is well known that this verse alludes to a geometric principle, namely that a triangular figure has no shadow. So consider whether you can conceive of that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 32:**

﴿Indeed, it﴾: that is, the Fire, which is indicated by the context. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the branches (of smoke). ﴿Throws up sparks﴾: the *sharar* is what flies off from the fire. It is so named because of the belief that it is evil (*sharr*). It is a collective noun of the category of *ism jins*, whose singular is *sharara*. ﴿Like a castle﴾: like a large house, ﴿built high﴾. The meaning is that every spark is like this in size. What follows the verse indicates this meaning, and it is supported by the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam, *bi-shirarin*, with a *kasra* on the *shin* and an *alif* between the two *ra*'s. Apparently this is the plural of *sharara*, like *raqaba* and *riqab*, which indicates that what is compared to the castle is the single spark. Likewise is the recitation of 'Isa, *bi-sharar*, with a *fatha* on the *shin* and an *alif* between the two *ra*'s, also. It has been said that this is the plural of *sharara*, not a singular noun. It has also been allowed, according to the recitation with the *kasra*, that it may be the plural of *sharr* (evil) and not the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), like *khiyar*, the plural of *khayr*. In that case it is an adjective placed in the position of its noun, meaning: it throws up people who are evil. This, however, goes against the apparent meaning.

It has been said that *al-qasr* is the thick part of a tree, whose singular is *qasra*, like *jamra* and *jamr*. It has also been said that it refers to pieces of wood about a cubit long, more or less, prepared for winter, whose singular is likewise *qasra*. In that case the comparison is of plural to plural, without need for interpretation by what has passed. However, the terrifying effect according to the last opinion is less than according to the others.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam recited *kal-qasar* with a *fatha* on the *qaf* and the *sad*. This means the roots of palm trees, and it has been said that it means their necks (stems). Its singular is *qasara*, like *shajara* and *shajar*. In the *Kitab al-Nabat* it is stated: the seed has two layers; the inner one is called *qishra* and the outer one is called *qasra*. From this is the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿like the qasr﴾. This is a rare usage.

Ibn Mas'ud recited *kal-qusur* with two *damma*s, the plural of *qasr*, like *rahn* and *ruhun*. In al-Bahr it is said: it seems to be a shortened form of *qusur* (palaces), like *najm* (star) and *nujum*. This goes against the apparent meaning, because such a form is either a poetic necessity or an irregular, rare usage.

Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also recited *kal-qisar* with a *kasra* on the *qaf* and a *fatha* on the *sad*, the plural of *qasara*, with two *fatha*s, like *halaqa* (a ring of iron) and *halaq*, and *haja* and *hiwaj*. Some reciters recited *kal-qasir* with a *fatha* on the *qaf* and a *kasra* on the *sad*, and this has the same meaning as *al-qasr* in the recitation of the majority.

"As if it were" — that is, the sparks — "yellow camels" (jimalat, with a kasra on the jim, as read by Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i and Harun from him). It is the plural of jamal (camel), and the ta' marbuta is for the feminine plural, as mentioned in al-Bahr: one says jamal, jimal and jimala. Or it is a collective noun (ism jam') for it, as was said of hajar and hijara. The tanwin indicates multiplicity. "Yellow" (sufr): the sparks, because of their fiery and airy nature, are yellowish, so sufr keeps its well-known meaning.

It has also been said that they are black (sud), and the expression "yellow" is used because the blackness of camels tends toward yellow, resembling the sparks as they separate from the fire in their size (by the qasr, the palm-like huge spark) and as they begin to rise and spread out, since they split into countless numbers, likened to camels in the conception of splitting and multitude, in the yellowness and in the particular movement. The order in the comparison has been observed, in consideration of the order of existence. I note that the palace-like (qasr) and the camels are compared to one another, and among this is his saying:

"So I stopped there with my she-camel, as if she were a fadan (a stone-built hut) for the one who waits to fulfil his need."

The second comparison is an explanation of the first, in the sense that the comparison with the qasr was what came first to understanding in terms of size alone; so when it was said "as if it were yellow camels," which stands in place of specification of the qasr, the aspect of resemblance was multiplied, as if it were said: "as if it were a palace of such and such qualities." The comparison with camels also includes multitude, succession, and rapidity of movement. The first is the verified view, according to al-Kashshaf, and on both views the second comparison is not a repetition at all, and there is no need on either to consider that the pronoun in "ka'annahu" refers to the qasr. He has touched on something of the beauty of the comparison occurring in the verse. Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri, in his saying in an elegy for one of the nobles:

"Those who kindle the fire of hospitality at evening and at dawn, by generosity and by hospitality,
crimson, blazing in its tufts in the darkness, throwing out every spark like a tiraf."

Even if he intended by this to rival the verse, then Allah the Exalted has blinded his insight to the excellence in it, as He blinded his sight.

Al-Jumhur, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim and with alif and ta', the plural of jimal, or jimala with a kasra on the jim in both, so it is the plural of the plural or the plural of a collective noun; the meaning is as you have heard.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' (with variation from them) read it likewise, except that they put a damma on the jim, as the plural of jumala, according to al-Kashshaf. In al-Bahr it is said: it is the ropes of ships; the single one of them is jumla, because it is a bundle (jumla) of strands, then it was pluralized as jumal and jimal, then jimal was pluralized again as the sound feminine plural, so they said jimalat. It has also been said it is the thick cables of bridges, i.e. the ropes with which they are tied; this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, who said that when they gather in a circle, one against another, large bodies come from them.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: they are large pieces of copper. The apparent meaning is that the comparison on this view concerns colour, and on the earlier view concerns extension and coiling.

Ibn 'Abbas also, along with al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ruways read "jumalat" like the reading of Hafs and those with him, except that they put a damma on the jim; according to al-Zamakhshari it is a singular noun meaning qals (a ship's cable), and the plural of "sufr" is for the purpose of the genus. al-Hasan read "sufur" with a damma on the fa'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 34–35:

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ ﴿This is a Day on which they will not speak.﴾ The reference is to the time of their entry into the Fire, meaning: this is a Day on which they will not speak anything, because of the magnitude of the terror and the extreme of bewilderment. This does not contradict what is related in another place about their speaking, because the Day of Resurrection is long and has stations (mawatin) and appointed times (mawaqit). In some of them they speak, and in some of them they do not speak. It is also permitted that the meaning is: this is a Day on which they will not speak anything that benefits them, and their speaking, since it brings no benefit, is treated as if it were no speech at all.

Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa, Abu Haywa and 'Asim, in one narration, read «هَذا يَوْمَ» with a fatha. It is said that this is the fatha of i'rab (grammatical case), with hadha being a demonstrative referring to what was mentioned, and «yawma» being in the accusative as a time adverb (zarf), related to an omitted element that occurs as the predicate (khabar) of hadha, meaning: this which was mentioned of the threat occurs on a Day when they will not speak. It is also said that this is the fatha of construction (bina'), and yawma is in the nominative position as the predicate, and it was built because it is attached to a clause, and because it is by nature something that should be built. From the author of al-Lawami', it is reported that 'Isa said: the building of «yawma» on the fatha together with la is the dialect of Lower Mudar, because they treated it as a single word with la. You know that the Basran grammarians do not permit, for an adverb attached to a clause beginning with an affirmative or negative present-tense verb, any form of building; and what has been mentioned is a Kufan opinion.

﴿And they will not be permitted﴾. It is said that this refers to speech in general, or to making excuses. Zayd ibn 'Ali, as reported from him by Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi, read it in the active voice, meaning: "And Allah, exalted is He, will not permit them" ﴿so they will not make excuses﴾. The clause ﴿so they will not make excuses﴾ is conjoined to "will not be permitted" and is included with it under the negation. The fa' (فاء) indicates sequence between the two negations in terms of reporting, according to one opinion, or it indicates that the second negation itself follows from the first, according to another. This was considered. The verb was not put in the subjunctive (naṣb, the subjunctive mood) as "fa-ya'taḍiru" would be after a negation. It is said that the purpose is for the speech to convey the negation of making excuses in every sense, since they have no excuse, and they do not make excuses. This differs from what would be the case if it were put in the subjunctive and made a response (jawab), for then it would indicate that their not making excuses is due to their not being permitted, which would give the false impression that they had an excuse but were not permitted to offer it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The verb was not put in the subjunctive after the negation only in order to preserve the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayy, the rhyme-endings of the verses), and both readings are permissible. Its apparent meaning is that the meaning is the same under both readings. This contradicts their statements, since they hold that the subjunctive has a causal sense (sababiyya) while the indicative (raf', the nominative mood) does not. Yes, Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam held that the verb may be in the indicative and its meaning, though rare, may be the meaning of the subjunctive after the fa'. He held that the grammarians only made the meaning of the indicative different from that of the subjunctive out of regard for what is most common in Arabic speech. He took this verse as evidence for that position. Ibn 'Usfur and others refuted him, so reflect on this.

The apparent meaning is that the negation of making excuses applies to some times and occasions, just as the negation of speech does. It is also permitted that the negated thing is the true, beneficial excuse, so there is no contradiction between what is here and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ [Ghafir: 52].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 37–38:

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ ﴿This is the Day of Decision (al-Fasl)﴾ between the one who is in the right (al-Muhiqq) and the one who is in the wrong (al-Mubtil). ﴿We have gathered you and the former peoples.﴾ That is, those who came before you of the nations. And the statement is an affirmation and clarification of the decision (al-fasl), because there is no separating between the one in the right and the one in the wrong except when they are gathered together.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verse 39–40:

﴿So if you have a stratagem, then use it against Me.﴾ Indeed, all of those whom you used to follow and imitate are present here. This is a rebuke to them for their scheming against the believers in the world, and a demonstration of their helplessness. ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ Because it has become clear that they have no power and no means of escaping what they are in.

﴿Indeed the God-fearing﴾ (al-muttaqun) are those who are protected from disbelief and denial, since they are placed in opposition to the deniers of the Day of Judgment. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 45–46:

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ For their enemies have obtained this great reward, while they remain in the painful punishment. ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed, you are criminals."﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the deniers, according to what many of the eminent scholars (al-ajilla) have held: that is, woe is established for them in a state in which it is said to them this, as a reminder of what was said to them in the world, and of what they were deserving of being addressed with, since they abandoned the abundant share for the paltry, base portion. Thus it conveys reproach (tahsir) and causing of loss (takhsir). Following this same manner is his (the poet's) saying:

"My brothers, do not be far away forever; but yes, by God, they have indeed gone far."

So this is a supplication for his brothers that they not be destroyed after their destruction, affirming that they were deserving of that supplication during their lives, and that their destruction was due to the appointed term reaching its end, not because they were deserving of being cursed.

Abu Hayyan, however, held that it is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʼnaf) addressed to the deniers in the world, and the matter in it is one of reproach, threat and causing of loss. The threat was not taken into account in the first view, because it is not intended in the Hereafter. This view was preferred on the grounds that it is further from forced interpretation (ta'assuf) and more suited to the coherence of the arrangement (ta'lif al-nazm), but there is room for consideration in this. The apparent meaning is that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿indeed you﴾ and so on, is in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil), and in it is an indication that the final end of every criminal is the enjoyment of a few days, after which he remains in punishment and destruction forever.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 47–48:

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down,"﴾ meaning: obey Allah, the Exalted, and humble yourselves and submit to Him, Mighty and Majestic, by accepting His revelation, the Exalted, and following His religion, the Glorified, and abandon this arrogance and haughtiness. ﴿They do not bow down.﴾ That is, they do not humble themselves, nor do they accept that; rather they persist in the arrogance they are upon. It was also said: that is, when they are commanded to pray or to bow in it, they do not do so. For it was narrated from Muqatil that "this verse was revealed concerning Thaqif. They said to the Messenger, may the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him: 'Remove the prayer from us, for we will not pay the tribute, and it would be a disgrace upon us.' He, may the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him, said: 'There is no good in a religion that has no bowing or prostration.'" Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani and others also narrated it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "This is on the Day of Resurrection, when they will be called to prostrate, but they will not be able to prostrate, because they did not prostrate in the world."

The connection of the verse, as transmitted from al-Zamakhshari, with the statement of the Exalted ﴿to the deniers﴾ is as if it were said: "Woe on that Day to those who denied, and those who, when it is said to them, 'Bow down,' do not bow down." It is also permitted that it connects with the statement of the Glorified ﴿Indeed, you are criminals﴾ by way of iltifat (shift of address), as if it were said: "They are worthy that it be said to them, ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves﴾," then He gave the reason for that by their being criminals and by their being, when it is said to them, "Pray," not praying. It was used as evidence that the command implies obligation and that the disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings (al-furu').

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 77, verses 49–50:**

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ ﴿Then in what statement after it will they believe?﴾ That is, after the Qur'an, which speaks of the news of the two abodes and the reports of the two creations, in a wondrous and inimitable style, founded on decisive proofs and manifest demonstrations, ﴿will they believe?⁠﴾ since they did not believe in it. The expression "after it" (*ba'dahu*), rather than any other word, serves to alert that no statement equals it in excellence, comes near to it in virtue, or surpasses and exceeds it. Therefore no statement is more deserving of belief than it. Thus *ba'd* indicates a difference in rank, as they said regarding ﴿ʿutullin baʿda dhalika zanim﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. The *fa'* (then) is used because the meaning is: since the matter is so, and the Qur'an includes the sufficient explanation and the clear truth, what is the matter with them that they do not hasten to believe in it before the opportunity passes and the woe descends, and they gain nothing from "perhaps," "maybe," and "would that"?

Ya'qub and Ibn 'Amir, in one narration, read *tu'minun* ("you believe") in the second person, as an address.

When he was brief in Surat al-Insan regarding the states of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and expansive in describing the states of the believers there, he reversed the matter in this surah. Thus balance was achieved between these two surahs. And Allah knows best.
